summary:
Región de Tarapacá stands under Chile's national statutory framework, which is among the more developed in the region. Legal gender recognition has operated since 2019 on a self-determination basis with no medical or surgical conditions attached. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and since 2012 the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences. Birth certificates also offer a third sex option for intersex children.

The controlling risk for a transgender visitor to Tarapacá is judicial rather than statutory. In early October 2023 the Court of Appeals of Iquique annulled in whole the trial of Jhonatan Cañon for the 2022 murder of trans woman Yuri Pizarro in Tarapacá, holding that the offence of femicidio covers only 'a person biologically female'. The conviction could not stand as framed, which voids the strongest gendered-violence protection available in the penal code within the territory where that court exercises jurisdiction. A trans woman killed in Tarapacá therefore cannot be protected by the charge that carries the heaviest penalty for gender-motivated killing.

Case volume in the region is small in absolute share but rising. Movilh's XXIII Annual Human Rights Report, published in March 2025 with 2024 data, places Tarapacá at about 2% of nationally documented homo/transphobic cases and among the fastest-rising regions, at +18.18% year-on-year, with growth also flagged at +19.51% in the report's period tables. The practical reading is a documented and widening protection gap against gender-motivated violence rather than a high absolute case load.

Detention carries specific protections nationally. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing trans detainees recognition of their assumed gender, including placement and segmented housing by gender identity, rules on entry examinations and access for trans visitors, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives monitoring implementation.

Violence against trans people is documented and recent. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing and was described in the national press as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.
tangentialFactors:
The policy record nationally has stalled. A Chilean advocacy group's annual assessment judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights, the first such reversal since the return of democracy in 1990, attributing the failure of equality and trans-rights bills to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction. Movilh's 24th Annual Human Rights Report, published in 2025, describes a breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus around LGBTIQ+ rights, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers.

The Iquique annulment is a narrowing produced by judicial interpretation, not by a change in the statute: the femicide provision remains on the books with its wording intact, and the Court of Appeals read it restrictively. Whether other courts in Chile adopt the same biological reading is not sourced here, so the reach of the gap beyond Tarapacá is unresolved.

Institutional hostility is visible inside state employment. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging she was relegated to administrative duties, had her private life exposed without consent, and was denied support.

Tarapacá's roughly 2% share is small against the national total, so the region reads as a rising-trend data point within a national pattern rather than as an outlier of volume; the +18.18% and +19.51% growth figures both come from the same Movilh report and are not reconciled there.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tarapacá access legal gender recognition through the national self-determination procedure in force since 2019, with no medical or surgical condition required, and may register a third sex marker on birth certificates for intersex children.

Same-sex marriage, joint adoption and civil unions are available nationally, and the criminal code aggravates hate-motivated offences on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity, a provision in force since 2012.

Trans people held in custody in the region are covered by the Gendarmería de Chile protocol on recognition of assumed gender, segmented housing by gender identity, entry examinations and access for trans visitors, monitored by a standing committee with undersecretariat representatives.

Residents face the same evidentiary gap as visitors: the Court of Appeals of Iquique's 2023 reading of femicidio as limited to 'a person biologically female' removes the aggravated charge in the killing of a trans woman within the region.

Employment protection is contested in practice. Isabella Panes's 2025 suit against Carabineros alleges reassignment to administrative duties, non-consensual exposure of her private life and refusal of support.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome after the annulment is unresolved: whether Jhonatan Cañon was retried, convicted on another basis, or the proceedings remain open is not stated in the sources held here.

Whether the Court of Appeals of Iquique's biological reading of femicidio has been appealed, upheld or cited by other Chilean courts is not sourced, so its reach outside Tarapacá is unverified.

The Movilh report gives a share and growth rates but no absolute case count for Tarapacá; the number of documented homo/transphobic cases in the region is not available from the inventory. The +18.18% and +19.51% figures are not reconciled within the report as summarised.

No region-specific source covers Tarapacá other than the Movilh report, so enforcement of the Gendarmería protocol, local police practice and access to trans-competent care in the region are not sourced.

The national press characterisation of the 2023 killing of Ever as Chile's biggest hate crime is a media description, not a judicial finding, and no court outcome for that case is given here.
